<reason>Side A (CON) kept the stronger live route: concrete recidivism after jail releases vs speculative trust, plus the jail-as-safest-enforcement-point turnaround that sanctuary forces fear-producing field arrests. Its warrant-veto point that civil detainers cannot meet a criminal-warrant demand was never answered, and its real-as-enacted vs ideal framing blunted B's notification-concession trap. B's anecdote-vs-aggregate point was good but left core enforcement mechanics unrebutted, with a clipped opening as added cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's civil-detainer vs criminal-warrant veto in Rebuttal 1, answered with probable-cause standard in Rebuttal 2, which directly damaged B's claim that sanctuary already cooperates via judicial warrant and was never repaired.</best_rebuttal>
